result.markdown: # How this book is built {#sec-build} The good-practice chapter makes a case for projects, relative paths, a locked set of package versions and a build anyone else can reproduce. It would be a poor case if the book itself did not follow it, so here is the book itself, opened up. Where the arrangement is awkward, or where a choice is a judgement rather than a rule, that is said out loud. You need none of this to work through the book. You need it to rebuild the book, to fork it for another course, or to work out why a render failed. ## The repository ``` r-intro/ ├── _quarto.yml project and book configuration ├── _common.R sourced by every chapter, in a hidden chunk ├── _dependencies.R never sourced, never rendered; see below ├── .Rprofile one line, and renv wrote it ├── .gitignore short, and one character of it is load-bearing ├── .gitattributes keeps generated files out of diffs ├── LICENSE MIT ├── renv.lock exact versions of every package ├── renv/ activate.R, settings.json, and the library itself ├── index.qmd the front page ├── setup.qmd … the chapters, one file each ├── solutions.qmd the appendices, one file each ├── data.qmd ├── build.qmd this page ├── colophon.qmd ├── R/nus_theme.R the ggplot2 theme and the colour palette ├── scss/nus.scss the site styling, layered on bootswatch litera ├── scripts/check_palette.R the palette's accessibility tests ├── scripts/publish.sh render, then push the site to gh-pages ├── scripts/stamp-build.sh records which commit produced the site ├── scripts/check-pages-sync.sh is what is live still what main says? ├── scripts/hooks/pre-push reminds you that pushing is not publishing ├── assets/ favicon, and the three footer logos ├── data/sg_covid_data.csv the dataset, all 23 kB of it └── _freeze/ cached chunk output, committed on purpose ``` The rendered site is not in that list, and its absence is the whole publishing strategy; there is a section on it further down. `_freeze/` is generated and in version control anyway, which is unusual enough that it gets a section of its own too. One file per chapter, and the chapter list in `_quarto.yml` is the only place the reading order is written down. Renaming a file means editing `_quarto.yml`, and forgetting to means the chapter silently disappears from the book while still sitting in the repository. It is the most common way to lose a page. ## `_quarto.yml`, section by section The whole build is one YAML file. It opens with a warning to future me: ```yaml # Verified against Quarto 1.4.554. The project: and book: schemas are closed, # so an unrecognised key there is a hard render failure — check # /Applications/quarto/share/schema/definitions.yml before adding one. ``` That is worth reading twice. Under `project:` and `book:`, Quarto validates keys against a fixed schema. A typo does not get ignored, and it does not warn. The render stops. The schema files shipped with your Quarto installation are the authority, and they are more reliable than a blog post about a different version. ### `project:` ```yaml project: type: book execute-dir: project post-render: - scripts/stamp-build.sh ``` `type: book` is what turns a folder of `.qmd` files into a numbered book with parts, appendices, previous and next links, and a single search index. There is no `output-dir`, which is a decision rather than an omission. Quarto therefore renders into its default `_book/`, and `_book/` is gitignored, because the rendered site is not kept on this branch at all. What happens to it instead is the publishing section. `execute-dir: project` sets R's working directory to the project root for every chunk in every chapter. Without it, each chapter would execute in its own directory, which is fine here because every file sits at the top level, but stops being fine the moment anyone puts a chapter in a subfolder. Setting it means `here::here("data", "sg_covid_data.csv")` resolves identically from every chapter, including this one. `post-render:` runs `scripts/stamp-build.sh` after the last page is written. It drops a small `build-info.json` into the output recording which commit the site was rendered from. That file has a job, and the job only makes sense alongside the rest of the publishing arrangement, so it is explained there too. ### `book:` Metadata first: title, subtitle, author, `date: today` with an explicit `date-format`, and a description that becomes the page's meta description and the social preview text. `site-url` and `repo-url` together are what make the "Edit this page", "Report an issue" and "View source" links work. `repo-actions: [edit, issue, source]` turns all three on. They appear in the right-hand margin of every page, and they are the cheapest error-reporting mechanism a teaching resource can have. A student who spots a wrong number is two clicks from telling me, and one of those clicks lands them in a text editor with the offending line in front of them. `repo-branch: main` matters because Quarto builds the edit URL from it. Point it at a branch that does not exist and every edit link 404s, on every page, silently. Then the reading conveniences: `search: true`, `reader-mode: true` (the button that collapses both sidebars), `page-navigation: true` and `back-to-top-navigation: true`. The sidebar is docked rather than floating, collapsed to one level so the parts are visible but the sections are not, and carries two tools: a link to the source on GitHub, and a direct download link for the CSV. The download link points at `raw.githubusercontent.com`, not at the repository page, so it downloads the file instead of showing a preview of it. ### `chapters:` and `appendices:` ```yaml chapters: - index.qmd - part: "Before you write any code" chapters: - setup.qmd - good-practice.qmd ``` The parts are headings in the sidebar and nothing else; they carry no files of their own. `index.qmd` sits outside any part because a book's front page is not a chapter. `appendices:` is a separate list, and Quarto numbers it separately: chapters get 1, 2, 3, appendices get A, B, C, D. The `crossref: appendix-title: "Appendix"` setting at the bottom of the file is what makes a reference to one of them read "Appendix B" rather than just "B". ### `page-footer:` The footer carries the three institutional logos as a raw HTML block, plus the licence on the left and the Quarto credit and issue link on the right. The logos are `` tags pointing at `assets/logos/`, styled by a `.footer-logos` rule in `scss/nus.scss`. They are raster PNGs rather than SVGs because that is the artwork as supplied, and redrawing an institution's mark is not a thing to do casually. ### `format:` ```yaml format: html: theme: [litera, scss/nus.scss] ``` Bootswatch `litera` underneath, the project's own SCSS on top. `litera` was chosen for a reason that has nothing to do with taste: it is one of the few bundled themes that does not fetch a web font from `fonts.googleapis.com`. The book renders the same on a plane as it does on a fast connection. For a course whose first session is often held on university wifi, that is worth more than a nicer typeface. The rest of the HTML block, in the order it appears: `toc: true` with `toc-depth: 3` and a custom `toc-title`. `number-sections: true`, so sections can be referenced by number. `anchor-sections: true` gives every heading a link target, which is what lets me point a student at one paragraph rather than a chapter. `smooth-scroll: true` is cosmetic. `code-copy: true` puts a copy button on every code block. `code-overflow: scroll` gives a long line its own horizontal scrollbar rather than wrapping it, which is the less obvious choice of the two. This dataset has column names 49 characters long — `retail_and_recreation_percent_change_from_baseline` is one — and wrapping breaks them mid-identifier, so the name a student is meant to read and retype arrives in two halves. `code-link: true` is the good one. It turns every function call in every code block into a link to that function's documentation, so `filter()` in a chunk is clickable and lands on the dplyr reference page. It needs `downlit` and `xml2` installed. Neither is called by name anywhere in the book, so both are in the lockfile only because `_dependencies.R` names them, which is a trap the renv section comes back to. `code-annotations: hover` is how the numbered callouts in code blocks behave. `df-print: default` is a deliberate refusal. Set it to `kable` and every data frame in the book renders as a tidy HTML table with proper borders. It would look better. It would also look nothing like what the student sees in their own console, and a beginner comparing the book to their screen would conclude they had done something wrong. Console output stays console output. Figures: `fig-width: 7`, `fig-height: 4.2`, `fig-align: center`, `fig-format: svg`. SVG because plot text stays sharp at any zoom and the files are usually smaller than PNG for this kind of chart. `tbl-cap-location: bottom` follows the usual convention of captions below tables and above figures. ### `execute:` and why chapters must not fight it ```yaml execute: freeze: auto echo: true warning: true message: true ``` Warnings and messages are on, globally and on purpose. `read_csv()`'s column specification, `geom_histogram()`'s note about picking 30 bins, and `summarise()`'s `.groups` notice are all messages, and the book teaches students to read all three. A chapter that sets `message: false` to make its output tidy is deleting the lesson. Because these are set globally, chapters should not set them again. Repeating `#| echo: true` on a chunk is harmless but noisy; repeating it inconsistently is how a chapter ends up with three different behaviours for no reason anybody can reconstruct later. The same goes for `comment`, `collapse`, and the figure dimensions, all of which are set once in the `knitr:` block at the bottom: ```yaml knitr: opts_chunk: comment: "#>" collapse: true dev: "svg" ``` `comment: "#>"` prefixes every line of output. It means you can select a whole block, code and output together, paste it into your console, and have it run: the output lines are comments. `collapse: true` puts code and its output in one block rather than two. Two per-chunk options are used, and only these two. `#| eval: false` for anything that must not run during a render, which means `install.packages()`, `renv::` calls, `setwd()` demonstrations, `View()`. `#| error: true` for chunks that are supposed to fail, where the error message is the point. ## `_common.R` Every chapter opens with the same four lines: ```` ```{{r}} #| label: setup #| include: false source("_common.R") ``` ```` `include: false` hides the chunk and its output. The reader never sees it. The repetition is not laziness. Quarto's freeze machinery gives each chapter its own R session, which is what makes a single chapter re-renderable without re-running the whole book. A variable created in chapter 4 does not exist in chapter 5. So anything more than one chapter needs has to be defined in a file that every chapter sources, and `_common.R` is that file. It attaches the packages, sets the ggplot2 theme, defines `read_covid()` and `covid_daily()`, and runs the guard described in the next section. The leading underscore is a Quarto convention: files and directories starting with `_` are not treated as book content and are not copied to the output. ## renv, and the one that will get you `renv` records the exact version of every package the book was built with. It does this in `renv.lock`, a JSON file with one entry per package: ```json "here": { "Package": "here", "Version": "1.0.2", "Source": "Repository", ... "Repository": "CRAN" }, ``` (Trimmed. Each real entry also carries the package's title, licence, dependencies and maintainer.) The lockfile is a manifest, not a copy of the packages. It is a few hundred kB of text that says which versions to go and get. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} lock <- renv::lockfile_read() lock$R$Version #> [1] "4.6.1" length(lock$Packages) #> [1] 109 ``` ::: 109 packages, for a book whose `_common.R` calls `library()` four times. Almost all of them are dependencies of dependencies, which is the honest reason to use a lockfile at all: nobody can hold that graph in their head, and "install the tidyverse" resolves to a different set of versions every month. The three commands you need: `renv::restore()` reads the lockfile and installs exactly those versions into `renv/library`. This is the first thing to run in a fresh clone. It takes a few minutes once. `renv::status()` compares what is installed against what is recorded, and tells you which way they disagree. `renv::snapshot()` writes the current state back into the lockfile. Run it after adding a package, and commit the resulting diff along with the change that needed it. The library itself is not in version control. renv writes and maintains `renv/.gitignore` for you: ``` library/ local/ cellar/ lock/ python/ sandbox/ staging/ ``` `renv.lock`, `renv/activate.R` and `renv/settings.json` are tracked. Those three plus the ignore rules are what makes a clean checkout reproducible without committing several hundred megabytes of compiled code. `.Rprofile` is one line, and renv wrote it: ```r source("renv/activate.R") ``` R runs `.Rprofile` from the working directory at startup. That line activates the project library, and it is the whole mechanism. ### `_dependencies.R` renv finds dependencies by scanning source files for `library()` calls. Its scanner automatically adds `rmarkdown` when it sees `.Rmd` files, but not for `.qmd`. This book has no `.Rmd` files, so without intervention `renv::snapshot()` leaves `knitr` and `rmarkdown` out of the lockfile entirely, and a clean checkout fails to render with an error that points nowhere near the cause. `_dependencies.R` is a file that exists only to be scanned. It is never sourced and never rendered. It lists the packages the chapters use plus the ones the toolchain needs but nothing calls by name: `knitr`, `rmarkdown`, `downlit`, `xml2`, `sessioninfo`. If you add a package to a chapter, add it there too, or it will work on your machine and nowhere else. ### The gotcha This is the one that cost me an evening. Quarto decides which renv to activate by reading `.Rprofile` **relative to the directory you invoked it from**, not relative to the project you asked it to render. So this is fine: ```bash cd ~/r-intro quarto render ``` and this is not: ```bash cd ~/sph5421-course # another R project, with its own .Rprofile and its own renv quarto render ../r-intro ``` The second one starts R in `~/sph5421-course`, reads that project's `.Rprofile`, activates that project's library, and then renders this book against whatever versions happen to be sitting there. `execute-dir: project` moves the working directory afterwards, so `here()` and every relative path still work, and the render completes. That is what makes it dangerous. The versions in a neighbouring project are usually close enough that most of the book builds, and you find out three chapters later when a `dplyr` deprecation warning appears on a page that never had one. So `_common.R` checks, before it does anything else: ```r local({ proj <- getwd() while (!file.exists(file.path(proj, "_quarto.yml")) && dirname(proj) != proj) { proj <- dirname(proj) } expected <- normalizePath(file.path(proj, "renv", "library"), mustWork = FALSE) active <- normalizePath(.libPaths()[1], mustWork = FALSE) if (!startsWith(active, expected)) { stop( "Wrong package library.\n", " active: ", active, "\n", " expected: ", expected, "/...\n", "Run `quarto render` from the project root (", proj, ").", call. = FALSE ) } }) ``` It walks up from the working directory until it finds `_quarto.yml`, works out where that project's library ought to be, and compares it against the library R is actually using. When they disagree the render stops on the first chapter with: ``` Error: Wrong package library. active: /Users/you/sph5421-course/renv/library/macos/R-4.6/aarch64-apple-darwin25.4.0 expected: /Users/you/r-intro/renv/library/... Run `quarto render` from the project root (/Users/you/r-intro). ``` The two paths will be yours. The fix is always the same: `cd` into the project root and render from there. Here is the library this page was built against: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} .libPaths()[1] #> [1] "/Users/swapnil/Documents/GitHub/r-intro/renv/library/macos/R-4.6/aarch64-apple-darwin25.4.0" ``` ::: If that path does not contain `r-intro/renv`, the guard has a bug, which would also be worth an issue. ## Freeze `freeze: auto` means a chapter's R code is executed when the chapter's `.qmd` changes, and not otherwise. The output of every chunk is cached under `_freeze/`, and `_freeze/` is committed. The payoff is that anyone can clone the repository and rebuild the site without R, without renv, and without the several minutes of computation. It also means a one-word fix to chapter 9 does not re-execute chapters 1 through 8, which turns a two-minute render into a five-second one and is the difference between previewing your changes and not bothering. The cost is a trap. **Freeze watches the `.qmd` file, not the things it depends on.** Edit `_common.R`, change the colour palette in `R/nus_theme.R`, or replace the CSV, and nothing re-runs. The book will render happily and every page will still show the old output. There is no warning, because from Quarto's point of view nothing changed. There is no command-line flag to force it. When you have changed something shared, delete the cache: ```bash rm -rf _freeze/ quarto render ``` or delete one chapter's directory under `_freeze/` if you know that only one is affected. Doing this after any change to `_common.R` is a habit worth building, and the reason `_freeze/` is listed in `.gitattributes` as generated is that the resulting diff is enormous and nobody should read it. ## Publishing `main` holds the source and nothing else. The rendered site lives on a branch of its own, `gh-pages`, which carries the built HTML and nothing else, and that is the branch GitHub Pages is configured to serve. Rendering locally puts the book in `_book/`, which is gitignored, so you can build and reread it as often as you like without git ever noticing. Publishing is one command: ```bash ./scripts/publish.sh ``` It renders the book and hands the result to `quarto publish gh-pages --no-prompt`, which pushes the output onto `gh-pages`. Then it checks what actually went out: that the expected number of pages exist, that no page got stranded at the project root, that `search.json` is present, since a missing search index makes the search box return nothing rather than fail visibly, and that every `solutions.html#sec-sol-…` link in the book has an anchor waiting for it in `solutions.html`. In a book that cross-links every exercise to its worked answer, a dead link is a worse defect than a failed render, because a failed render tells you. It refuses to start in three cases. If a `quarto preview` is running, because the preview watches the same files, races the render, and has left the output half-moved. If you are not on `main`. And if the working tree is dirty, which is the interesting one and needs the next section first. ### What the split buys, and what it costs The reason to keep the site off `main` is diffs. Generated HTML is not source. A re-render rewrites every page, so fixing two words in one chapter arrives as a commit touching ninety files, and `git log` on that chapter becomes something you scroll past rather than read. It gets worse than untidy as soon as a second person edits chapters, because HTML merges badly: two people who touched different chapters still both regenerated the whole site, and git offers you conflicts in dozens of files nobody can resolve by reading them. With the output on its own branch, a chapter edit is a one-file diff, and a merge is a merge of prose. The cost is real and worth naming, because the previous arrangement was better at one thing. When the site was committed alongside the source, forgetting to rebuild was impossible to miss: you edited a chapter and the working tree stayed dirty until you rendered. Staleness announced itself for free. Split source from output and that goes away. `main` is clean whether or not you have ever published. You can edit a chapter, commit, push, watch GitHub show your change, and have the live site still serving last month's text with nothing anywhere hinting at it. That is a quiet failure of exactly the kind this book keeps warning about, and it is why the three small scripts below exist. They are compensation for the visibility the split threw away. `scripts/stamp-build.sh` runs as the `post-render` step and writes `build-info.json` into the output: the commit HEAD was at, whether the tree was dirty at the time, the build timestamp, and the Quarto version. Rendered HTML has no idea which revision of the source produced it, and this is how it is told. `scripts/check-pages-sync.sh` reads that file off `gh-pages` and compares the commit in it against the tip of `main`. It exits 0 in sync, 1 when the site is stale, and 2 when it cannot tell — no `gh-pages` branch yet, no `build-info.json` in it, no network. `--local` skips the fetch and works with the refs you already have. `publish.sh` runs it at the end as its own last check. The part of that script worth copying is the part that stays quiet. It does not compare commit counts. It compares the *files* that changed since the publish against a list of things the rendered site is actually built from — the `.qmd` files, `_quarto.yml`, `_common.R`, `R/`, `scss/`, `data/`, `assets/` — and if the only commits since were a README edit or a licence tweak, the site is still correct and it says so. A check that shouted "stale" every time you fixed a typo in a comment would be ignored inside a week, and an ignored check is worse than no check, because it leaves you believing something is being watched. `scripts/hooks/pre-push` prints a reminder when the commits you are pushing touch anything on that list. It is not installed by default; enable it with: ```bash git config core.hooksPath scripts/hooks ``` It prints and gets out of the way. It does not block the push, and that is deliberate: pushing source before publishing is a perfectly normal thing to do, and a hook that refused would be routed around with `--no-verify` the second time it got in the way, after which it may as well not exist. Which is where the dirty-tree rule in `publish.sh` comes back. Render with uncommitted changes and the stamp names a commit that does not contain what was rendered, so every check downstream is reasoning from a false statement — the sync check compares against source that was never published and reports agreement that is not there. `stamp-build.sh` does record `"dirty": true` when it happens, and the sync check treats that as stale outright rather than pretending, but refusing to publish from a dirty tree in the first place is cheaper than either. ### No CI, still There is no GitHub Action here, and the reason has not changed. This book is built with Quarto 1.4.554, on one laptop, against a package library pinned by `renv.lock`. Any route that renders on a server adds a second Quarto at a second version, and a newer Quarto does not fail loudly on an older book. It produces slightly different HTML from the version the book was checked against, which is a category of bug you find weeks later on one page. Publishing from here keeps the render on the machine the versions are pinned to, and only the output travels. ### `.nojekyll`, and why this repository does not have one GitHub Pages runs Jekyll over your site by default, and Jekyll ignores every file and directory whose name begins with an underscore. Quarto's HTML output is full of them. An empty `.nojekyll` at the root of the published site turns Jekyll off entirely, and without it the site deploys with no CSS at all, which looks exactly like a broken theme and is not. The published site has one. This repository does not, and there is nothing under `project: resources:` copying one into the output either, because Quarto writes that file itself during `quarto publish` and puts something in it: a deploy id, which it reads back from the live site afterwards to confirm that what is being served is the copy it just pushed. Ship your own `.nojekyll` and you overwrite that id, and the verification fails on a deploy that worked perfectly. ### The leading slash in `.gitignore` ``` # Chapters render to the project root before Quarto moves them into _book, so # a failed render can leave them behind. The leading slash matters: unanchored, # `*_files/` would also match the figure directories inside the output. /*_files/ ``` Knitr writes a chapter's figures into `_files/` next to the source, and Quarto moves them into the output directory at the end of the render. A render that dies partway through leaves them sitting at the project root, and those working directories are rubbish that should not be in git. The obvious rule is `*_files/`. The obvious rule is wrong. A pattern with no slash at the start matches at **any depth**, so `*_files/` also matches `_book/visualise_files/`, `_book/groups_files/`, and every other directory in the rendered site that holds the actual published images. Git would ignore all of them, and the output still goes through git on its way out — that is what publishing to a branch is. The failure this used to cause was memorable enough to be worth keeping the guard for: render, see a perfect book on `localhost`, publish, and get a live site where every plot is a broken-image icon, with nothing in the local build ever showing it. The leading slash anchors the pattern to the repository root, so it matches `./visualise_files/` and stops there. One character. `.gitattributes` finishes the job, marking the generated directory so it stays out of GitHub's language statistics and out of diffs: ``` _freeze/** linguist-generated=true _freeze/** -diff ``` Without it, GitHub reads the repository as mostly generated JSON and SVG rather than R, and re-running one chapter arrives as a pull request with thousands of changed lines that nobody should be asked to review. ## Forking it The licence says you can, so here is how. ```bash git clone https://github.com/CERM-NUS/r-intro.git my-course cd my-course ``` Open `r-intro.Rproj` in RStudio. The `.Rproj` file keeps its old name after a clone, so rename it now if the old one will confuse you later. Then, in the R console: ```r renv::restore() ``` Answer yes. Go and make coffee. When it finishes, from a terminal **in that directory**: ```bash quarto preview ``` That builds the book and opens it in a browser with live reload: save a `.qmd` and the page updates. It is the right mode for writing. `./scripts/publish.sh` is the one for shipping, and it will refuse to run while a preview is still going, so stop the preview first. Four things to change before you publish your version: `_quarto.yml` needs a new `site-url`, `repo-url` and probably `repo-branch`, or every edit link on your site will point at mine. The logos in `assets/logos/` have to go, or be replaced with your own. They are the trade marks of NUS, the Saw Swee Hock School of Public Health, CERM and the ML & GHN network, and the MIT licence on the text and code does not cover them. Remove the `page-footer` HTML block along with the files. `LICENSE` should keep the original copyright line if you keep any of the original text, and add yours. If you swap the dataset, `_common.R` is the only place that reads it, but `data.qmd` documents the columns of *this* file and will be wrong the moment you change it. Rewrite that appendix or delete it. An out-of-date data appendix is worse than none. Then commit your sources, push, and run `./scripts/publish.sh`. That creates the `gh-pages` branch the first time it runs, and once it has, go to the repository's Pages settings and set it to deploy from `gh-pages`. Until you do that last step the branch exists and nothing serves it.
